Empirical Research Plan  
“Does attending a more‐selective college raise earnings?”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen design: Instrumental-Variables (2SLS).  
Why IV?  
• OLS comparisons suffer from selection on unobservables (ability, ambition, family networks).  
• The C&B file records, for each student, (i) the complete set of colleges applied to, (ii) which colleges admitted the student, and (iii) which one the student eventually attended.  
• Conditional on the portfolio of schools applied to, whether a given campus admits the student contains a substantial idiosyncratic component (departmental quotas, reader idiosyncrasies, enrollment management, etc.).  
• We therefore use “admission to a more-selective college” as an instrument for “attendance at a more-selective college.”  The first stage is strong, and the exclusion restriction is plausible once we control for student SAT, high-school GPA, demographics, and fixed effects for the application portfolio.

Basic 2SLS layout  
First stage:  SelectivityAttendedᵢ = π· SelectivityAdmittedᵢ + Xᵢβ + εᵢ  
Second stage:  ln(Earningsᵢ) = α· ŜelectivityAttendedᵢ + Xᵢγ + uᵢ

where SelectivityAdmittedᵢ = average (or maximum) selectivity of the colleges that admitted student i but that she did not necessarily attend.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: SelectivityAttendedᵢ = percentile rank (0–100) of the college’s median SAT score or Barron’s index.  
• For some robustness checks, define a binary treatment: Top-25% college = 1 if the campus’s selectivity percentile ≥ 75.

Control group / counterfactual  
• Students who, given the same application portfolio, were not admitted to (or did not attend) a more-selective college.  
• In binary specifications, untreated = college selectivity < 75th percentile.

Timing  
• Treatment occurs at initial matriculation in fall 1976; outcomes (earnings) are observed in 1991–93.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Relevance: Admission outcomes are strongly correlated with where the student enrolls.  
 Plausibility: Historically, yield rates are high; F-stat > 10 is expected.

A2. Independence (quasi-random admission shocks): Conditional on the set of colleges applied to and rich covariates, which campuses admit the student is as-good-as random with respect to unobserved earnings potential.  
 Plausibility: Most campuses used holistic but noisy processes; multiple campuses read identical files independently.

A3. Exclusion: Admission to a more-selective college affects later earnings only through the college actually attended, not through other channels (e.g., psychological confidence).  
 Plausibility: Harder to guarantee, but controlling for the quality of all schools applied to mitigates concerns.

A4. Monotonicity: No student would attend a less-selective college when she would have attended a more-selective one had the latter admitted her (direction of causal impact of the offer is weakly positive).  
 Plausibility: Reasonable—financial aid aside, being admitted to a highly-selective college cannot reduce the likelihood of attending one.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One student’s admission outcome does not influence another’s earnings in this cohort.  
 Plausibility: Cohort is large but dispersed across 30+ campuses; interference minimal.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Non-random application sets  
 Problem: Ambitious students may apply to more‐selective schools AND earn more regardless.  
 Fix: Include fixed effects for the entire application set (or coarse groups such as average selectivity of all schools applied to). In practice, create dummies for the average SAT selectivity decile of the application portfolio.

T2. Omitted ability measures (e.g., unobserved motivation) correlated with both admission probabilities and future earnings.  
 Fix: Control flexibly for student SAT scores, high-school GPA, extracurricular index, parental education & income. Show balance tests on these observables between instrumented treatment and control sub-samples.

T3. Weak instrument or violation of exclusion via financial aid interactions.  
 Fix: (a) Report first-stage F-stat. (b) Use alternative instruments—e.g., “number of offers from top-quartile colleges”—to show consistent results. (c) Conduct a placebo test using earnings measured before college (parent income) to verify null effect.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS
library(modelsummary) # nice tables
library(sandwich)    # robust vcov

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# -------------------------------------------------
cb <- read_csv("college_and_beyond_1976.csv")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# -------------------------------------------------
cb <- cb %>%
  mutate(
    # Selectivity measures supplied in data
    sel_attend  = college_selectivity_percentile,                   # 0–100
    top25_attend = (sel_attend >= 75),
    
    # Instrument: mean selectivity of schools that admitted the student
    sel_admit = admitted_colleges_selectivity_mean,                 # assumes pre-computed
    top25_offer = (sel_admit >= 75),
    
    ln_earn = log(earnings_1992),                                   # outcome
    
    # controls
    sat       = student_sat,
    sat2      = student_sat^2,
    gpa_hs    = highschool_gpa,
    female    = (gender == "Female"),
    black     = (race == "Black"),
    hisp      = (race == "Hispanic"),
    parent_inc = log(parent_income_1975 + 1)
  ) %>%
  drop_na(sel_attend, sel_admit, ln_earn)          # keep complete cases

# Fixed effects for application portfolio decile
cb <- cb %>%
  mutate(app_portfolio_decile = ntile(applied_colleges_selectivity_mean, 10) %>% factor())

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS specification
# -------------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ sel_attend + sat + sat2 + gpa_hs + female + black + hisp + parent_inc | 
    app_portfolio_decile ~ sel_admit,
  data = cb, 
  vcov = "hetero"
)

summary(iv_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness check: alternative binary instrument
# -------------------------------------------------
iv_binary <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ top25_attend + sat + sat2 + gpa_hs + female + black + hisp + parent_inc | 
    app_portfolio_decile ~ top25_offer,
  data = cb, 
  vcov = "hetero"
)

# Weak-instrument F-statistic
etable(iv_main, iv_binary, fitstat = c("ivfstat"))

# Placebo: effect on parental income (should be 0)
iv_placebo <- feols(
  parent_inc ~ sel_attend | app_portfolio_decile ~ sel_admit,
  data = cb, 
  vcov = "hetero"
)
summary(iv_placebo)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory: More-selective colleges provide better peer effects, alumni networks, and signaling value ⇒ positive earnings premium.  
Prior magnitude: Dale-Krueger-style estimates ≈ 0–10 % higher earnings for a 20-percentile increase in selectivity. I expect a semi-elasticity of roughly 0.003–0.005 log-points per selectivity percentile, i.e., attending a 90th-percentile vs. 50th-percentile institution raises earnings about 12–20 %.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Instrument relevance (First-stage F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable after controls …………… 0  
C3: Independence from potential outcomes given portfolio … 1  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ……………………………………… 1  
C5: No selective attrition in earnings reporting ……………… 0  

Total = 3 / 5 ⇒ credible but not bulletproof; results should be interpreted as LATE for compliers.
